passages.rooftop: Rooftop gardens have become increasingly common in large cities over the past two decades. Originally, they were built mainly to make buildings look more attractive, but their practical benefits are now better understood. A layer of soil and plants on a roof absorbs rainwater, which reduces the pressure on drains during storms. It also keeps a building cooler in summer, so less electricity is needed for air conditioning. In some cities, residents grow vegetables on shared roofs and sell them at local markets. However, building a rooftop garden is not cheap. The roof must be strong enough to carry the weight of wet soil, and a waterproof layer has to be installed to prevent leaks. For this reason, most gardens appear on new buildings rather than old ones. Supporters argue that the long-term savings on energy and water outweigh the initial cost.
